issues.title: [Python] Numpy constraint is present in the build but not in the runtime constraints
issues.body:
### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.

Here https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/apache-arrow-26.0.0/python/pyproject.toml#L25 we have:
```toml
[build-system]
requires = [
    "numpy>=2.0",
]
```
For the project dependencies, there do not appear to be any mentioned that I can see. However, when I run the code, I see:
```
  File ...
    import pyarrow as pa
  File ...
    from pyarrow.lib import ...
  File "pyarrow/lib.pyx", line 42, in init pyarrow.lib
ImportError: pyarrow requires NumPy 2.0 or newer, found 1.26.4
```
when I use `pyarrow==26.0.0`. 

It seems to me that there is a missing dependency that should be present to constraint the numpy version in the runtime dependencies (alongside the build time ones). 

### Component(s)

Python
issues.author: oliversheridanmethven

comments.body:
I can confirm the behaviour and the version boundary (Python 3.12.15, Linux x86_64, `uv pip install`):

| pyarrow | numpy 1.26.4 |
|---|---|
| 21.0.0, 22.0.0, 23.0.1, 24.0.0, 25.0.1 | `import pyarrow` works, `pa.array(np.arange(3)).to_numpy()` works |
| 26.0.0 | `ImportError: pyarrow requires NumPy 2.0 or newer, found 1.26.4` |

The 26.0.0 wheel's `METADATA` has no `Requires-Dist` lines at all, so pip/uv have nothing to resolve against.

Some context in case it helps: this was an intentional change for 26.0.0 in #50769 (GH-48473, "Require numpy 2.0"). The check is in `pyarrow/lib.pyx` (lines 40-45 at `apache-arrow-26.0.0`) and only runs if `import numpy` succeeds. NumPy is still an optional runtime dependency. With numpy uninstalled, pyarrow 26.0.0 imports fine, and a Parquet write/read round trip and `pc.sum` work. That's probably why there's no runtime requirement. Adding `numpy>=2` to `[project].dependencies` (what #53971 proposed; it was closed without being merged) would make numpy mandatory for everyone, and package metadata has no way to say "numpy>=2, but only if numpy is installed".

The [install docs for 26.0.0](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/install.html#dependencies) already list "NumPy 2.0 or higher" under *optional* dependencies, which matches this behaviour.

Practical options for now: `pip install "numpy>=2"` alongside pyarrow 26, or pin `pyarrow<26` if you need to stay on NumPy 1.x. On the user side, a constraints file with `numpy>=2` also does the job. I tried this in a fresh Python 3.12 venv with `-c constraints.txt`:

- `pyarrow==26.0.0` alone: numpy is not installed
- `pyarrow==26.0.0 "numpy<2"`: resolution fails (pip and uv both)
- `pyarrow==26.0.0 pandas==2.2.3`: numpy 2.5.4 is picked (uv)

A constraint doesn't upgrade a numpy 1.x that's already installed if you only install pyarrow, though (checked with uv). In that case you still have to upgrade numpy yourself.

issues.title: [Parquet][Python][Dataset] Mixed FileInfo and path sources can crash Python in dataset()
issues.body:
### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.

### Describe the bug

`pyarrow.dataset.dataset()` behaves inconsistently when its source list contains both filesystem paths and `pyarrow.fs.FileInfo` objects.

Both homogeneous input types work correctly. However, mixed inputs behave differently depending on their order:

- `[path, FileInfo]` raises a normal `TypeError`.
- `[FileInfo, path]` terminates the Python process.

The crash occurs instead of a safe Python exception.

### Reproduction

```python
import pathlib
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import textwrap

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

child_code = textwrap.dedent("""
    import sys
    import pyarrow.dataset as ds
    import pyarrow.fs as fs

    path, case = sys.argv[1:3]
    info = fs.LocalFileSystem().get_file_info(path)

    sources = {
        "paths_only": [path, path],
        "infos_only": [info, info],
        "path_first": [path, info],
        "info_first": [info, path],
    }[case]

    print("Starting:", case, flush=True)

    try:
        result = ds.dataset(
            sources, format="parquet"
        ).to_table().to_pydict()
        print("Result:", result, flush=True)
    except Exception as exc:
        print("Exception:", type(exc).__name__, str(exc), flush=True)
""")

print("Python:", sys.version.split()[0])
print("PyArrow:", pa.__version__)
print("Platform:", sys.platform)

with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    path = pathlib.Path(directory) / "tiny.parquet"
    pq.write_table(pa.table({"x": [1]}), path)

    for case in ("paths_only", "infos_only", "path_first", "info_first"):
        run = subprocess.run(
            [sys.executable, "-X", "faulthandler", "-c",
             child_code, str(path), case],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            timeout=30,
        )
        print(case, "returncode:", run.returncode)
        print("stdout:", run.stdout.strip())
        print("stderr:", run.stderr.strip())
```

### Actual behavior

Observed with PyArrow 23.0.1 on Kaggle/Linux:

```text
paths_only: returncode 0
infos_only: returncode 0
path_first: TypeError: not a path-like object
info_first: returncode -11
Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault
```

The same four-case assessment was repeated with PyArrow 26.0.0, where both homogeneous cases succeeded, path-first raised `TypeError`, and FileInfo-first terminated the subprocess.

The behavior was also reproduced locally on Windows with PyArrow 16.1.0 and 24.0.0.

### Expected behavior

Mixing file paths and `FileInfo` objects should either:

1. Be supported consistently in both orders; or
2. Raise a clear Python exception in both orders.

Invalid or unsupported source combinations should not terminate the interpreter.

### Possible root cause

In `python/pyarrow/dataset.py`, the public `dataset()` function accepts lists containing either paths or `FileInfo` objects, but the downstream `_filesystem_dataset()` logic dispatches based on the first element.

When the first element is `FileInfo`, the native `FileSystemDatasetFactory` receives a mixed list. Its Cython path assumes the remaining entries are also `FileInfo` objects, which appears to cause the native crash.

A possible minimal fix is to reject mixed lists safely before entering native code. Alternatively, mixed inputs could be normalized if supporting them is the intended API contract.

I'd appreciate maintainer guidance on the preferred behavior.

### Environment

- Kaggle/Linux, Python 3.13.15, PyArrow 23.0.1
- Kaggle/Linux, PyArrow 26.0.0
- Windows, PyArrow 16.1.0 and 24.0.0

The investigation and initial report drafting were AI-assisted. I independently ran and reviewed the Kaggle reproductions.

### Component(s)

Python, Parquet

issues.title: [Python] Process aborts at interpreter exit: `~PyReadableFile` takes the GIL on a ThreadPool worker during finalization (`pd.read_parquet` on a local path)
issues.body:
### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.

A short-lived process that reads a local parquet file through pandas and then exits sometimes aborts with SIGABRT (exit 134), after all of its work and output are done. stderr shows `terminate called without an active exception` and `Fatal Python error: Aborted`, with no Python frame.

pandas opens a Python file handle for a local path and passes it to the dataset reader, which wraps it in a `PyReadableFile`. A reader task can drop the last reference on a ThreadPool worker thread while the interpreter is finalizing. `OwnedRefNoGIL::~OwnedRefNoGIL` then calls `PyGILState_Ensure`, CPython ends the thread with `pthread_exit`, the forced unwind passes a noexcept destructor, and `std::terminate` is called.

**Reproduction**

```python
# write.py: run once
import pandas as pd
pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [1.0, 2.0]}).to_parquet("p.parquet", index=False)
```

```python
# read.py: run many times, a few in parallel
import pandas as pd, sys
pd.read_parquet(sys.argv[1], columns=["a", "b"])
print("ok")
```

```
python write.py
seq 3000 | xargs -P 4 -I{} sh -c 'python read.py p.parquet >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo $?' | sort | uniq -c
```

Expected: no output (every run exits 0). Observed: `38 134`, that is 38 of 3000 runs abort.

The same loop with `pyarrow.parquet.read_table(sys.argv[1], columns=["a", "b"]).to_pandas()` in place of `pd.read_parquet` gives no output, so 0 of 3000 runs abort. The file is then opened natively, and no Python object is held by the reader.

**Environment**
- pyarrow 26.0.0 (pyarrow 25.0.1 aborts at the same rate)
- pandas 3.0.6, numpy 2.5.3
- CPython 3.12.12
- Debian 12 (bookworm), aarch64, in Docker

**Stack of the aborting thread (gdb)**

```
#0  __pthread_kill_implementation
#3  abort
#4  __gnu_cxx::__verbose_terminate_handler()
#6  std::terminate()
#7  __gxx_personality_v0
#9  _Unwind_ForcedUnwind
#10 __pthread_unwind
#12 __pthread_exit
#13 PyThread_exit_thread
#14 take_gil
#15 PyEval_RestoreThread
#16 PyGILState_Ensure
#17 arrow::py::OwnedRefNoGIL::~OwnedRefNoGIL()
#18 arrow::py::PyReadableFile::~PyReadableFile()
#19 std::_Sp_counted_base<...>::_M_release_last_use_cold()
#20 std::_Function_handler<arrow::Result<std::shared_ptr<arrow::io::RandomAccessFile>>(), arrow::dataset::FileSource::FileSource(...)>
#21 arrow::dataset::FileSource::~FileSource()
#22 arrow::dataset::ParquetFileFragment::~ParquetFileFragment()
... on a ThreadPool worker thread (ThreadPool::LaunchWorkersUnlocked)
```

**Possible fix.** Skip the decref in `OwnedRefNoGIL`'s destructor when the interpreter is finalizing (`Py_IsFinalizing()`), as other C++ extensions do. Alternatively, release the scan's fragments on the calling thread before `read_table` returns.

**Related.** ARROW-16597 has the same mechanism in Flight: `PyThread_exit_thread` → `pthread_exit` while C++ code is on the stack, at interpreter exit.

### Component(s)

Python
issues.author: yo-han

comments.body:
Additional reproduction on the current released wheels, run with Codex assistance on the designated remote workstation (Linux x86_64, CPython 3.12.15, PyArrow 26.0.0, pandas 3.0.6):

- 2 of 300 fresh subprocesses using `pandas.read_parquet` aborted with signal 6 and `terminate called without an active exception`.
- 0 of 300 control subprocesses using `pyarrow.parquet.read_table(...).to_pandas()` aborted.

This is on x86_64, not the reporter's aarch64 platform, but it reproduces the same exit-time failure on the Python-file-handle path.

issues.title: [Python][Parquet] ParquetFile projection includes extra column when dotted field name matches nested path
issues.body:
### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.

### Describe the bug

`pyarrow.parquet.ParquetFile.read()` returns an unexpected extra column when a literal top-level column name contains a dot and collides with a nested field path.

For example, a Parquet file contains two distinct fields:

- `a.b`: a literal top-level column.
- `a`: a struct containing nested field `b`.

When requesting `columns=["a.b"]`, `ParquetFile.read()` returns **both** `a.b` and `a`, whereas `pq.read_table()` returns only `a.b`.

I independently reproduced this in Kaggle using **PyArrow 26.0.0**. The behavior was also observed locally with PyArrow 16.1.0 and 24.0.0.

### Minimal reproduction

```python
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

print("PyArrow version:", pa.__version__)

table = pa.table({
    "a.b": [10, 20],
    "a": pa.array([{"b": 1}, {"b": 2}]),
    "other": [3, 4],
})

sink = pa.BufferOutputStream()
pq.write_table(table, sink)
data = sink.getvalue()

file_result = pq.ParquetFile(
    pa.BufferReader(data)
).read(columns=["a.b"])

table_result = pq.read_table(
    pa.BufferReader(data),
    columns=["a.b"],
)

print("ParquetFile.read:", file_result.column_names, file_result.to_pydict())
print("pq.read_table:", table_result.column_names, table_result.to_pydict())
```

### Actual behavior

```text
PyArrow version: 26.0.0
ParquetFile.read: ['a.b', 'a'] {'a.b': [10, 20], 'a': [{'b': 1}, {'b': 2}]}
pq.read_table:    ['a.b'] {'a.b': [10, 20]}
```

### Expected behavior

Column projection should have a clear and consistent interpretation across the Parquet reading APIs.

Preferably, specifying `columns=["a.b"]` should select the exact top-level column named `a.b` when it exists, without unexpectedly including the unrelated top-level struct `a`.

Alternatively, if this name is considered ambiguous, a clear error or an explicit path-selection mechanism may be more appropriate.

I would appreciate maintainer guidance on the intended precedence.

### Possible root cause

In `python/pyarrow/parquet/core.py`, `_build_nested_paths()` constructs lookup keys by joining path components with `"."`.

This makes the following distinct physical paths indistinguishable as strings:

```text
["a.b"]    -> "a.b"
["a", "b"] -> "a.b"
```

Consequently, `_get_column_indices()` can select both physical columns for a single requested name.

### Impact

This may cause unexpected output schemas, unnecessary Parquet column reads, additional memory usage, or downstream failures in applications that use dotted column names alongside nested structures.

### Environment

- PyArrow: 26.0.0
- Platform: Kaggle notebook (Linux)
- Reproduction: In-memory Parquet buffer; no external files or datasets required.

I can prepare a focused regression test and fix once the expected ambiguity-resolution behavior is clarified.

The investigation and initial report drafting were AI-assisted; I independently executed and reviewed the reproduction.

### Component(s)

Parquet, Python

issues.title: [Python][Parquet] Writing a sparse union column raises ArrowNotImplementedError
issues.body:
### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.

`pyarrow.parquet.write_table` refuses a table with a sparse union column, whether the union is at the top level or nested in a list or struct:

```python
import io

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

union = pa.UnionArray.from_sparse(
    pa.array([0, 1], type=pa.int8()),
    [pa.array([1, None]), pa.array([None, "x"])],
    field_names=["a", "b"],
)
pq.write_table(pa.table({"u": union}), io.BytesIO())
```

```
pyarrow.lib.ArrowNotImplementedError: Unhandled type for Arrow to Parquet schema conversion: sparse_union<a: int64=0, b: string=1>
```

`pa.ListArray.from_arrays([0, 2], union)` and `pa.StructArray.from_arrays([union], names=["f"])` raise the same error.

pyarrow 26.0.0 and 25.0.1, Python 3.14, macOS arm64.

#28288 reported the same error for dense unions and was closed as stale without a resolution.

Parquet has no union type, but a sparse union's children are each as long as the union, so it maps onto a group of its children plus a type-code column. The stored Arrow schema (`ARROW:schema`) could then restore the union on read, as it already restores `duration` written as `INT64`. If write support is out of scope, documenting the limitation would help.

This issue was drafted with an AI assistant, which also ran the reproducer on pyarrow 26.0.0 and 25.0.1. I reviewed it before filing.

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

Parquet metadata and schema equality can terminate the Python interpreter when the other operand is `None`. For example, checking `metadata.row_group(0).column(0).statistics == None` causes SIGSEGV instead of returning `False`.

The `equals()` methods accept a typed Cython object without rejecting `None`, then access its native pointer. `FileMetaData.equals()` already uses `other not None`; the other five metadata/schema classes do not.

### Reproducer

Run in an isolated Python process:

```python
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

sink = pa.BufferOutputStream()
pq.write_table(pa.table({"value": [1, 2, 3]}), sink)
metadata = pq.read_metadata(pa.BufferReader(sink.getvalue()))
statistics = metadata.row_group(0).column(0).statistics
print(statistics == None)  # process exits with SIGSEGV
```

The same result occurs with `.equals(None)`, row-group metadata, column-chunk metadata, and column schemas. On Arch Linux / CPython 3.14.8, `ParquetSchema` comparison also crashes. On Ubuntu / CPython 3.12.14 it happens to return `False`. This was reproduced with PyArrow 26.0.0 and with the current main `_parquet` extension built from source at `9b34c4a6a8856212b885f6a1e934795af04f3192` against the matching 26.0.0 SDK.

Expected: normal equality with `None` returns `False`; explicit `.equals(None)` rejects the invalid argument with `TypeError`, consistently with `FileMetaData`.

### Existing work checked

Open PRs #51161 and #51163 change other Parquet entry points (constructors, sorting, binary types). Their current patches do not change these five `equals()` methods. Searches for metadata/schema/statistics comparison and None-related open PRs found no overlapping fix.

Python, Parquet

issues.body:
### Describe the enhancement requested

For now this is more of a wishlist/discussion issue, but could grow into a more precise meta-task if we want to move forward.

There have been growing concerns over the years over the fragility of software supply chains, particularly when open source software is concerned. Some standards and practices have been proposed to help prevent such attacks:
* [SLSA](https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.0/) (apparently pronounced "salsa") is, AFAIU, a specification that help projects evaluate and improve their build and test practices
* Software bills of materials (SBOM) are a type of artifact that precisely describe the provenance of code shipped within a package (related link: announcement of a ["SBOM for Python packages" project](https://discuss.python.org/t/sboms-for-python-packages-project/70261); also: [Accelerating SBOM success with the help of SLSA](https://slsa.dev/blog/2022/05/slsa-sbom)) 
* [OpenSSF scorecards](https://securityscorecards.dev/) provide a standard vocabulary to evaluate a software projects' security practices
* [Reproducible builds](https://reproducible-builds.org/) help ensure that binary artifacts have not been compromised, by allowing independent verification of build outputs

Arrow C++ in particular has a non-trivial set of dependencies that are incorporated in the build process in various ways. For example, for Python wheels we use vcpkg on a specific changeset, potentially with home-grown patches. This of course applies to other bindings of Arrow C++ where we may produce binary packages (such as R).

We should evaluate whether any of these could help us improve our intrinsic quality, or would merely amount to additional bureaucracy (related link: [concerns by a prominent member of the Python packaging community](https://discuss.python.org/t/sboms-for-python-packages-project/70261/8)).

issues.title: [Python] DataFrame interchange silently corrupts non-native-endian columns.
issues.body:
### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.

### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.

`pyarrow.interchange.from_dataframe` can return incorrect values for columns
whose interchange-protocol dtype uses non-native endianness. The importer
interprets the producer's data buffer as native-endian without accounting for
the endianness field. No error is raised; the values are silently corrupted.

This was reproduced with PyArrow `26.0.0 (development build)` on macOS arm64
with Python 3.13.15. The same issue can affect non-native-endian string offset
buffers.

### Reproduction

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow.interchange as pai

df = pd.DataFrame({"value": np.array([1, 2, 300], dtype=">i4")})
table = pai.from_dataframe(df)
print(table["value"].to_pylist())
```

### Actual behavior

On a little-endian platform, this prints values interpreted with the wrong byte
order, for example:

```text
[16777216, 33554432, 738263040]
```

### Expected behavior

The imported values should preserve the producer's values:

```text
[1, 2, 300]
```

### Proposed fix

Convert non-native-endian data and string offset buffers to native byte order
when copying is allowed. If conversion requires a copy and `allow_copy=False`,
raise a `RuntimeError`.

Python

issues.title: [C++][Python] CSV: option to pad short rows with nulls instead of failing
issues.body:
### Describe the enhancement requested

Add an option to the CSV reader to read rows that have fewer fields than the number of columns, and fill the missing fields with null. pandas' C engine does this when `names` is given, and DuckDB has `read_csv(..., null_padding = true)`.

Today the width is fixed by `column_names`, or by the first row. A shorter row is an error, and `invalid_row_handler` can only skip it or stop. It cannot keep the row.

```python
import io
import pyarrow as pa
from pyarrow import csv

data = b"a,b\n1,2,3,4\n5,6,7,8\n"
names = ["w", "x", "y", "z"]

csv.read_csv(io.BytesIO(data), read_options=csv.ReadOptions(column_names=names))
# ArrowInvalid: CSV parse error: Expected 4 columns, got 2: a,b

csv.read_csv(io.BytesIO(data), read_options=csv.ReadOptions(autogenerate_column_names=True))
# ArrowInvalid: CSV parse error: Expected 2 columns, got 4: 1,2,3,4

csv.read_csv(io.BytesIO(data),
             read_options=csv.ReadOptions(column_names=names),
             parse_options=csv.ParseOptions(invalid_row_handler=lambda r: "skip"))
# {'w': [1, 5], 'x': [2, 6], 'y': [3, 7], 'z': [4, 8]}  -- the short row is dropped, not padded
```

Expected, with the new option:

```
{'w': ['a', '1', '5'], 'x': ['b', '2', '6'], 'y': [None, '3', '7'], 'z': [None, '4', '8']}
```

Real files have this shape. For example, the AEMO (Australian electricity market) daily CSV files mix record types: the first row is a short header record, and the data rows are wider. pandas with `engine="pyarrow"` cannot read them, because pandas uses Arrow's reader and Arrow takes the width from the first row. pandas marked this as an Arrow limitation: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/71034

The same request was #27832, closed as stale in January 2026. #28421 added `invalid_row_handler`, but it can only skip or error.

Tested with pyarrow 26.0.0, Python 3.12, Linux.

issues.title: [Python] String array buffer factories reject valid 64-bit counters
issues.body:
### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.

`StringArray.from_buffers()` and `LargeStringArray.from_buffers()` reject valid 64-bit array counters with `OverflowError: value too large to convert to int`. Their `length`, `null_count` and `offset` arguments are declared as C `int`, although the underlying Arrow `ArrayData` counters are `int64_t` and `Array.from_buffers()` accepts the same buffers.

Minimal example isolating an offset above INT32_MAX (64-bit POSIX; the mapping reserves address space without materializing billions of strings):

```python
import mmap
import struct
import pyarrow as pa

offset = 2**31
mapping = mmap.mmap(-1, (offset + 2) * 8,
                    flags=mmap.MAP_PRIVATE | mmap.MAP_ANONYMOUS)
struct.pack_into("<q", mapping, (offset + 1) * 8, 1)
offsets = pa.py_buffer(mapping)
data = pa.py_buffer(b"x")

array = pa.Array.from_buffers(pa.large_string(), 1, [None, offsets, data],
                             null_count=0, offset=offset)
assert array[0].as_py() == "x"  # valid, expected

pa.LargeStringArray.from_buffers(1, offsets, data,
                                null_count=0, offset=offset)
# OverflowError: value too large to convert to int
```

The same mismatch occurs for `StringArray`, and for valid arrays with lengths or null counts above INT32_MAX. Verified on PyArrow 26.0.0, Ubuntu/Python 3.12.14 and native Arch/Python 3.14.8. Rebuilding the original Python binding from current upstream source reproduces all six factory/counter cases. Generic controls can read the actual final values. Peak process RSS in these sparse-buffer checks is about 57–79 MiB.

Widening all three counters to `int64_t` in both helpers makes the specialized factories accept the same valid arrays. Normal string/binary buffer round-trips, six new regressions, and the array test module pass in both environments. There is no buffer-layout change.

Existing issue/PR searches found #49717 (buffer safety documentation) and historical #1772; neither addresses these counter widths. This report, reproduction and candidate patch were prepared with Codex and independently AI-reviewed; no human review is claimed.

issues.title: [C++][Parquet] Writer emits an empty first data page for a repeated column when data_page_size is small, and the reader then drops the row group's rows
issues.body:
### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.


When the first write batch of a list/map column chunk contains a single record, the Parquet writer can begin the column chunk with a data page that holds no values (`num_values = 0`, `num_rows = 0`). This happens when `data_page_size` is small. The Arrow reader takes that empty page as the end of the column chunk, so every row of that row group is silently missing on read, while the file metadata still counts them. DuckDB and Polars skip the empty page and read the rows.

This happens with a one-row file, and with any file whose last row group (or any row group, e.g. `row_group_size=1`) holds exactly one row.

**Reproducer**

```python
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

list_bool = pa.list_(pa.bool_())

# 1) one-row table
t = pa.table({"c0": pa.array([[True]], list_bool)})
pq.write_table(t, "one_row.parquet", data_page_version="2.0", data_page_size=64)
print(pq.ParquetFile("one_row.parquet").metadata.num_rows)   # 1
print(pq.read_table("one_row.parquet").num_rows)             # expected 1

# 2) the last row group holds a single row
t = pa.table({"c0": pa.array([[True], [False], [True]], list_bool)})
pq.write_table(t, "last_rg.parquet", data_page_version="2.0", data_page_size=64,
               row_group_size=2)
print(pq.read_table("last_rg.parquet")["c0"].to_pylist())    # expected [[True], [False], [True]]

# 3) default encoding (dictionary), any dictionary-encodable leaf type, V1 pages, very small page size
t = pa.table({"c0": pa.array([[1], [2], [3]], pa.list_(pa.int32()))})
pq.write_table(t, "dict.parquet", data_page_size=4, row_group_size=2)
print(pq.read_table("dict.parquet")["c0"].to_pylist())       # expected [[1], [2], [3]]

# 4) with a second column the read fails instead
t = pa.table({"id": [1], "c0": pa.array([[True]], list_bool)})
pq.write_table(t, "two_cols.parquet", data_page_version="2.0", data_page_size=64)
pq.read_table("two_cols.parquet")
```

Output on main:

```
1
0
[[True], [False]]
[[1], [2]]
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid: Column 1 named c0 expected length 1 but got length 0
```

DuckDB 1.5.x and Polars 2.0 read `one_row.parquet` as `[[True]]` and `last_rg.parquet` as all three rows. With `write_page_index=True`, ClickHouse refuses the file because the offset index lists two pages with the same first_row_index 0 (the empty page at offset 4, size 26, then the real page at offset 30, size 32): `Invalid offset index: PageLocation(offset=30, compressed_page_size=32, first_row_index=0), prev offset: 30, prev row: 0`.

I decoded the page headers of `one_row.parquet`. The column chunk holds two `DATA_PAGE_V2` pages: first `num_values=0, num_nulls=0, num_rows=0, encoding=RLE` with a 4-byte body (only the RLE length prefix), then the real page with `num_values=1, num_rows=1`.

**Scope** (main, a column chunk whose first write batch holds one record):

| leaf / encoding | `data_page_size` values that lose the row |
|---|---|
| BOOLEAN leaf with V2 data pages (RLE encoding) | 1 to 69 |
| any dictionary-encodable leaf with dictionary encoding (the default), V1 or V2 pages | 1 to 6 |
| non-boolean leaf with `use_dictionary=False` | none |
| non-repeated columns | none |

The writer can also emit an empty page in the middle of a chunk. For example, 1025 one-element `list<bool>` rows with `data_page_size=64` produce pages of 1024, 0 and 1 values. Arrow happens to read that file correctly.

**Versions:** pyarrow 27.0.0.dev13 (nightly built from main at 9f03413), Python 3.12, Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu 22.04). With the released wheels, cases 1, 2 and 4 reproduce from 22.0.0 on, and case 3 from 23.0.0 on (on 22.0.0, dictionary encoding is affected only with V2 pages); 22.0.0 through 26.0.0 were tested. pyarrow 21.0.0 writes a single page and reads the row back correctly.

**Where it comes from**

- Writer: `DoInBatchesRepeated` calls `action(offset, check_page_limit_end_offset - offset, /*check_page_limit=*/true)` with zero levels when the last record of the batch starts at `offset`, which is always the case for a batch holding a single record ([column_writer.cc#L1219-L1224](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/parquet/column_writer.cc#L1219-L1224)). `CommitWriteAndCheckPageLimit` then calls `AddDataPage()` when `EstimatedDataEncodedSize() >= data_pagesize()`, without checking that anything is buffered ([column_writer.cc#L1835-L1846](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/parquet/column_writer.cc#L1835-L1846)). An empty encoder's estimate is not 0:
  - `RleBooleanEncoder` returns 4 + `RlePreserveBufferSize(0, 1)` = 4 + 65 = 69 bytes ([encoder.cc#L1754-L1756](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/parquet/encoder.cc#L1754-L1756), [encoder.cc#L444-L451](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/parquet/encoder.cc#L444-L451)).
  - The dictionary encoder returns 1 + 5 = 6 bytes ([encoder.cc#L499-L503](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/parquet/encoder.cc#L499-L503)).

  These numbers match the thresholds in the table above exactly.
- The zero-length call became possible with GH-47027 (#47032, first released in 22.0.0), which changed `if (offset < last_record_begin_offset)` to `if (offset <= last_record_begin_offset)`. The later rewrite in #47090 kept this behaviour.
- Reader: `HasNextInternal()` returns false when the next page has `num_buffered_values_ == 0` ([column_reader.cc#L776-L785](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/parquet/column_reader.cc#L776-L785)). So `ReadRecords` returns 0 on a leading empty page, and `LeafReader::LoadBatch` moves on to the next row group ([arrow/reader.cc#L510-L514](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/parquet/arrow/reader.cc#L510-L514)).

Possible fixes:
- Writer: do not call `AddDataPage()` when nothing is buffered (`num_buffered_values_ == 0`), or skip the zero-length `action` call.
- Reader: skip a data page with zero values instead of treating it as the end of the column chunk. This would make files already written by 22.0.0–26.0.0 readable by future readers only: pyarrow 21.0.0 also reads `one_row.parquet` written by main as 0 rows, so a reader-only fix does not help older readers.

**Impact:** `data_page_size` is a public writer option. With small values, rows of list/map columns written by `pq.write_table` silently disappear when the file is read back with `pq.read_table` or pandas `read_parquet`, while the metadata still reports them. Multi-column files fail to load. Found by differential testing of Parquet writers and readers.

### Component(s)

C++, Parquet, Python


### Component(s)

C++, Parquet

issues.body:
## Body

Hi, and first off — thank you for #50801/#50802! `RecordBatchReaderSourceNodeOptions` is exactly what I needed for a project bridging a generator-backed data source into Acero, and it's working great.

While using it, I noticed the source seems to drain a `RecordBatchReader` at full speed regardless of how quickly (or whether at all) the downstream consumer is actually asking for batches. I'm not sure if this is expected given the backpressure work still in progress in #47383, or a separate gap specific to this node — flagging it in case the repro is useful data either way, no urgency on my end.

### Repro

Pure pyarrow, no other dependencies:

```python
import time
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.acero as ac

N = 200
DELAY = 0.05  # simulate a producer that takes real time per batch
table = pa.table({"a": list(range(N))})
batches = table.to_batches(max_chunksize=1)
pulled_count = [0]

def gen():
    for i, batch in enumerate(batches):
        time.sleep(DELAY)
        pulled_count[0] = i + 1
        yield batch

reader = pa.RecordBatchReader.from_batches(table.schema, gen())
decl = ac.Declaration("record_batch_reader_source", ac.RecordBatchReaderSourceNodeOptions(reader))
out_reader = decl.to_reader()

t0 = time.monotonic()
out_reader.read_next_batch()          # one read to start the plan
print("after first read:", pulled_count[0])

# Never ask for another batch -- just watch what happens anyway.
for _ in range(10):
    time.sleep(0.3)
    print(f"{time.monotonic() - t0:.2f}s: pulled_count={pulled_count[0]}/{N}")
```

### Observed

```
after first read: pulled_count=1
0.36s: pulled_count=6/200
0.67s: pulled_count=12/200
0.97s: pulled_count=18/200
...
9.18s: pulled_count=171/200
```

`pulled_count` climbs steadily the entire time with no plateau, even though `read_next_batch()` is only ever called once. It reaches 200/200 well before anything downstream has asked for more than the first batch.

### Expected (maybe?)

Given `SourceNode`'s general backpressure machinery (`BackpressureOptions`, the `backpressure_future_` in the read loop), I'd have expected the read loop to eventually pause once enough unconsumed batches have piled up — though I understand `BackpressureOptions` isn't wired up by `Declaration.to_table()`/`.to_reader()` at all today (`pause_if_above` defaults to 0 / disabled), so maybe this is simply "working as currently designed, nothing to configure it with yet." Genuinely not sure whether this belongs under #47383's umbrella or is worth its own tracking — happy to help however's useful, and thanks again for the node, it's a real improvement for exactly the kind of custom-source bridging I'm doing.

- pyarrow: `26.0.0.dev175` (scientific-python-nightly-wheels)

issues.title: [C++][Python] CSV writer writes a null of a one-column table as an empty line, which `read_csv` skips by default, so null rows are lost on a round trip
issues.body:
### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.


The CSV writer emits a null cell as the unquoted `null_string`, which is empty by default. In a table with a single column, a null row therefore becomes an empty line. Arrow's CSV readers skip empty lines by default (`ParseOptions.ignore_empty_lines = True`), so writing such a table with default options and reading it back silently drops every null row. `ds.write_dataset(..., format="csv")` and `ds.dataset(..., format="csv")` behave the same.

**Reproducer**

```python
import io
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.csv as csv

t = pa.table({"c": pa.array([1, None, 3, None, 5], pa.int64())})
buf = io.BytesIO()
csv.write_csv(t, buf)
print(buf.getvalue())

back = csv.read_csv(io.BytesIO(buf.getvalue()))
print(back.num_rows, back["c"].to_pylist())   # expected 5 [1, None, 3, None, 5]

# string column: an empty string is quoted, a null is not
s = pa.table({"s": pa.array(["a", None, "", "b"])})
buf = io.BytesIO()
csv.write_csv(s, buf)
print(buf.getvalue(), csv.read_csv(io.BytesIO(buf.getvalue()))["s"].to_pylist())
```

Output on main:

```
b'"c"\n1\n\n3\n\n5\n'
3 [1, 3, 5]
b'"s"\n"a"\n\n""\n"b"\n' ['a', '', 'b']
```

The file has 5 data rows but reads back as 3; the rows no longer line up with their positions, and no error or warning is raised. The other options behave as follows:
- `quoting_style="all_valid"` and `"none"` give the same result.
- With `include_header=False`, a leading null becomes an empty first line.
- Reading with `ParseOptions(ignore_empty_lines=False)` recovers all 5 rows.
- pandas `read_csv` (default `skip_blank_lines=True`) also reads 3 rows.
- Polars and DuckDB happen to read 5.

For comparison, Python's `csv` module writes a lone empty field as `""` precisely so that the row is not an empty line (`csv.writer(f).writerow([None])` writes `""`).

**Expected behavior:** a table written by `write_csv` with default options reads back with the same rows from `read_csv` with default options. For example, the writer could emit a null in a row with a single column as a quoted empty string (`""`) or as some other non-empty marker, like the Python `csv` module does.

For non-string columns, quoting is lossless: with default reader options a quoted `""` already reads back as null (`ConvertOptions.quoted_strings_can_be_null = True`), e.g. `csv.read_csv(io.BytesIO(b'"c"\n1\n""\n3\n'))` gives `[1, None, 3]`. For string columns, quoting would make the null read back as an empty string, so the writer may prefer another marker there. Either way, it should not emit an empty line that the default reader ignores.

**Versions:** pyarrow 27.0.0.dev13 (nightly built from main at 9f03413), Python 3.12, Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu 22.04). The released pyarrow 21.0.0 through 26.0.0 wheels behave the same.

**Where it comes from**

- Both column populators copy `null_string_` followed by the end characters for a null, without quoting and regardless of the number of columns ([csv/writer.cc#L277-L286](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/arrow/csv/writer.cc#L277-L286) for `UnquotedColumnPopulator`, [csv/writer.cc#L413-L421](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/arrow/csv/writer.cc#L413-L421) for `QuotedColumnPopulator`).
- The reader's default is `ignore_empty_lines = true`. The option's own comment says that only with `false` does "an empty line represent a single empty value (assuming a one-column CSV file)" ([csv/options.h#L59-L61](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/arrow/csv/options.h#L59-L61)).

**Impact:** exporting and re-importing one-column data with pyarrow's default CSV options is common, for example a list of ids or a single selected column. Doing so silently loses every null row, which changes row counts and breaks positional alignment with other data. Found by differential testing of CSV round trips.

issues.title: [C++][Compute] Casting an all-null list array read from IPC to fixed_size_list segfaults (Take with out-of-bounds index on an empty child)
issues.body:
### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.


### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.

Casting a `list`/`large_list`/`list_view` array to `fixed_size_list` crashes the process with a segmentation fault when the array's null slots do not have the target length and the child (values) array is empty with no data buffer. A null list read back from IPC is enough to trigger it:

**Reproducer**

```python
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.ipc as ipc

t = pa.table({"c": pa.array([None], pa.list_(pa.int64()))})
sink = pa.BufferOutputStream()
with ipc.new_stream(sink, t.schema) as w:
    w.write_table(t)
col = ipc.open_stream(sink.getvalue()).read_all()["c"]
col.validate(full=True)                              # passes

print(col.cast(pa.list_(pa.int64(), 3)))            # expected [null]
```

Output on main:

```
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
```

The IPC file format crashes too, and so do arrays built with `from_buffers` whose zero-length child has a null data buffer (spec-valid for a zero-length array):

```python
child = pa.Array.from_buffers(pa.int64(), 0, [None, None])
arr = pa.ListArray.from_buffers(pa.list_(pa.int64()), 1,
                                [pa.py_buffer(b"\x00"), pa.array([0, 0], pa.int32()).buffers()[1]],
                                children=[child])
arr.cast(pa.list_(pa.int64(), 3))                   # segfault
```

| input | cast to `fixed_size_list<…>[3]` |
|---|---|
| `list`, `large_list` or `list_view` with one null slot and an empty child without a data buffer (from IPC or `from_buffers`) | segfault |
| any value type tried (`int64`, `timestamp[us]`) | segfault |
| the same array from `pa.array([None], …)` (the child gets an allocated, zero-length data buffer) | `[None]`, but index 0 is still read out of bounds |
| a null slot of the wrong length with a non-empty child, e.g. `[[1, 2, 3], None, [4, 5, 6]]` | correct |

We first hit this on a Polars-produced `large_list<timestamp[us]>` (Polars `to_arrow()`): a chunk holding a single null list with an empty child.

**Backtrace** (pyarrow 25.0.1, gdb):

```
#0  arrow::compute::internal::(anonymous)::FixedWidthTakeImpl<unsigned long, std::integral_constant<int, 64>, ...>::Exec(...)
#1  arrow::compute::internal::FixedWidthTakeExec(...)
...
#11 arrow::compute::Take(arrow::Datum const&, arrow::Datum const&, arrow::compute::TakeOptions const&, arrow::compute::ExecContext*)
#12 arrow::compute::internal::(anonymous)::CastVarToFixedList<arrow::LargeListType>::Exec(...)
```

**Versions:** pyarrow 27.0.0.dev13 (nightly built from main at 9f03413), Python 3.12, Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu 22.04, glibc 2.35). The released wheels 15.0.2, 17.0.0, 19.0.1, 21.0.0, 23.0.0, 25.0.1 and 26.0.0 crash the same way.

**Where it comes from**

- When a null slot does not have length `list_size`, `CastVarToFixedList::Exec` rebuilds the values with `Take`. `BuildTakeIndices` emits the valid index `0` for every element of a null slot ("just fill in the null slots with first value", [scalar_cast_nested.cc#L230-L251](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/arrow/compute/kernels/scalar_cast_nested.cc#L230-L251)).
- `Take` is then called with `TakeOptions::NoBoundsCheck()` ([scalar_cast_nested.cc#L279-L286](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/arrow/compute/kernels/scalar_cast_nested.cc#L279-L286)). If the child is empty, index 0 is out of bounds. With a null data buffer, `FixedWidthTakeImpl` dereferences a null pointer. With an allocated buffer, it reads padding, and the result is hidden because the slot is null.
- `pc.take` on the same empty child with null indices (`[None, None, None]`) works, so the bad indices come from the cast kernel.
- The kernel is registered for `list`, `large_list`, `list_view`, `large_list_view` and `map` sources ([scalar_cast_nested.cc#L516-L521](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/arrow/compute/kernels/scalar_cast_nested.cc#L516-L521)).

Possible fixes:
- Emit a null index for the elements of a null slot (append nulls in `BuildTakeIndices`) instead of `0`, so `Take` never reads the child for them.
- Or, when the cast child has length 0, build the output values with `MakeArrayOfNulls(child_type, length * list_size)` instead of calling `Take`.

**Impact:** any process that casts list columns to `fixed_size_list` (for example to build embedding or tensor columns) crashes on input read from IPC or Arrow Flight, or received over the C Data Interface from another library, as soon as one batch holds only null lists. The crash cannot be caught from Python.

issues.title: [C++] Casting a zoned timestamp to string (and the CSV writer) truncates UTC offsets that have seconds, so the written instant is wrong
issues.body:
### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.


`cast(timestamp[unit, tz] -> string)` formats a zoned timestamp as local wall time plus a `%z` offset. The wall time is computed with the zone's exact UTC offset, but `%z` prints only hours and minutes. When the offset has a seconds part, the text therefore names a different instant than the stored value, off by up to 59 seconds. Examples of such offsets: Africa/Monrovia until 1972 (−0:44:30), Europe/Dublin until 1916, Europe/Paris until 1911, and the local mean time (LMT) of every IANA zone before it adopted standard time. `pyarrow.csv.write_csv` (and `write_dataset(format="csv")`) converts columns with this cast, so CSV exports of such values are wrong, and every reader of the file, pyarrow included, loads the shifted instant. No error or warning is raised.

**Reproducer**

```python
import io
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc
import pyarrow.csv as csv

# 1960-06-01 12:00:00 UTC; Africa/Monrovia was at UTC-00:44:30 then
utc = pa.array([datetime(1960, 6, 1, 12, tzinfo=timezone.utc)], pa.timestamp("us", "UTC"))
ts = utc.cast(pa.timestamp("us", "Africa/Monrovia"))
print(ts[0].as_py())                        # 1960-06-01 11:15:30-00:44:30 (correct)

print(pc.cast(ts, pa.string())[0])          # cast to string

buf = io.BytesIO()
csv.write_csv(pa.table({"ts": ts}), buf)
print(buf.getvalue().decode())

back = csv.read_csv(io.BytesIO(buf.getvalue()),
                    convert_options=csv.ConvertOptions(column_types={"ts": pa.timestamp("us", "UTC")}))
print(back["ts"][0], "!=", utc[0])
```

Output on main:

```
1960-06-01 11:15:30-00:44:30
1960-06-01 11:15:30.000000-0044
"ts"
1960-06-01 11:15:30.000000-0044

1960-06-01 11:59:30+00:00 != 1960-06-01 12:00:00+00:00
```

`11:15:30` is the correct local time for offset −00:44:30, but it is printed next to `-0044`. Together they mean 11:59:30 UTC, 30 seconds off. DuckDB and Polars read the CSV as the same shifted instant. Other examples on main:
- Europe/Dublin 1900-06-01 12:00 UTC → `11:34:39-0025` (−21 s)
- Europe/Paris 1900-06-01 12:00 UTC → `12:09:21+0009` (+21 s)
- America/New_York 1880-06-01 12:00 UTC → `07:03:58-0456` (−2 s)

All units (s/ms/us/ns) are affected. Offsets that are whole minutes, and the `"UTC"` zone (formatted with `Z`), are correct.

**Expected behavior:** the string names the same instant as the stored value. Two ways to get there:
- Print the offset with its seconds (e.g. `-00:44:30`, as Python's `isoformat()` does).
- Format in UTC (`...Z`) when the offset is not a whole number of minutes, or always for the CSV writer.

**Versions:** pyarrow 27.0.0.dev13 (nightly built from main at 9f03413), Python 3.12, Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu 22.04). The released pyarrow 21.0.0 through 26.0.0 wheels behave the same.

**Where it comes from**

- `CastFunctor<StringType, TimestampType>::ConvertZoned` formats with `"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S%z"` for every zone other than `"UTC"` ([scalar_cast_string.cc#L196-L215](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/arrow/compute/kernels/scalar_cast_string.cc#L196-L215)). It formats through `TimestampFormatter`, i.e. `chrono::to_stream` on a zoned time ([temporal_internal.h#L167-L195](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/arrow/compute/kernels/temporal_internal.h#L167-L195)).
- The vendored `date` library implements `%z` as `duration_cast<minutes>(*offset_sec)` and prints `±hhmm`, dropping the seconds of the offset ([vendored/datetime/date.h#L6012-L6043](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/arrow/vendored/datetime/date.h#L6012-L6043)). The `%H:%M:%S` fields, by contrast, use the exact local time.
- The CSV writer converts each column with `compute::Cast(data, utf8())` ([csv/writer.cc#L131-L144](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/9f0341314ca96eb58081d4132c77b460d880b2b0/cpp/src/arrow/csv/writer.cc#L131-L144)), so it inherits the problem.

**Impact:** historical, genealogical or astronomical timestamps stored in a local zone are exported to CSV (or cast to string) with instants that differ from the table by up to 59 seconds, without any error. Tables loaded back from such files hold the shifted values. Found by differential testing of CSV round trips.

issues.title: [C++][Substrait] RelCommon.emit indices are not bounds-checked before they index the schema
issues.body:
`GetEmitInfo` passes every value in `RelCommon.emit.output_mapping` to both `FieldRef(map_id)` and the unchecked `input_schema->field(map_id)`. `ProcessEmitProject` does the same on the project path, where the value also indexes `proj_options.expressions`. With this implementation, a positive out-of-range index still reads past the end of a `FieldVector` and the process dies. For `-1`, Acero later rejects `FieldRef(-1)` with `ArrowInvalid`, but the unchecked schema lookup happens first. `ProcessExtensionEmit`, in the same file, already returns `Status::Invalid("Out of bounds emit index ", emit_idx)`.

```
read, emit [1, 0]      [DataType(double), DataType(int64)]
read, emit [5]            exit 139
read, emit [-1]           ArrowInvalid: No match for FieldRef.FieldPath(-1)
project, emit [5]         exit 139
aggregate, emit [1, 0]    exit 139
```

The last variant is why this is more than a check on malformed input: that plan is valid Substrait. Arrow's vendored proto has no `expression_references`, so Arrow drops the grouping keys and derives an empty aggregate schema. The plan's valid `[1, 0]` mapping is then out of range for that empty schema. That grouping-key loss is #50634. A bounds check would turn the process crash into an error that reports the rejected `[1, 0]` mapping; fixing #50634 is still required for the plan to run.

Rechecked with PyArrow `26.0.0.dev244+g79e074ace`, built from `main` at `79e074ace3a7c4ca26f211dfd84a1984ad53c362`, on macOS arm64. The two positive out-of-range cases and the aggregate case still exit 139; the negative case now returns `ArrowInvalid`. The original PyArrow 25.0.1 reproduction crashed for the negative case as well on macOS arm64 and Linux x86-64. The source is `cpp/src/arrow/engine/substrait/relation_internal.cc`.

<details>
<summary>Reproducer — one file, pyarrow only</summary>

```python
"""RelCommon.emit.output_mapping indices are used to index the input schema unchecked.

The control succeeds and the negative case is caught as `ArrowInvalid`. Run each variant in a process of its own because the other three terminate:
    for v in 0 1 2 3 4; do python3 emit_repro.py $v || echo "   exit $?"; done
"""
import json, sys
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.substrait as ps
from pyarrow._substrait import _parse_json_plan

SCHEMA = pa.schema([pa.field("c0", pa.int64(), nullable=False),
                    pa.field("c1", pa.float64(), nullable=False)])

def provider(names, schema=None):
    return pa.table({"c0": [1], "c1": [2.5]}, schema=schema or SCHEMA)

def ref(i):
    return {"selection": {"directReference": {"structField": {"field": i} if i else {}},
                          "rootReference": {}}}

def emit(m):
    return {"common": {"emit": {"outputMapping": m}}}

def read(m=None):
    r = {"baseSchema": {"names": ["c0", "c1"], "struct": {
             "types": [{"i64": {"nullability": "NULLABILITY_REQUIRED"}},
                       {"fp64": {"nullability": "NULLABILITY_REQUIRED"}}],
             "nullability": "NULLABILITY_REQUIRED"}},
         "namedTable": {"names": ["t"]}}
    return {"read": dict(r, **(emit(m) if m else {}))}

def run(rel, names):
    plan = {"version": {"minorNumber": 102, "producer": "repro"},
            "relations": [{"root": {"input": rel, "names": names}}]}
    return ps.run_query(_parse_json_plan(json.dumps(plan).encode()), table_provider=provider)

# A plan that is valid Substrait: the grouping keys are where current Substrait puts them.
# Arrow's vendored proto has no expression_references, so it drops them (#50634) and the
# aggregate's output schema has no fields at all - which puts a correct mapping out of range.
AGG = {"aggregate": dict({"input": read(),
                          "groupings": [{"expressionReferences": [0, 1]}],
                          "groupingExpressions": [ref(0), ref(1)]}, **emit([1, 0]))}

VARIANTS = [
    ("read, emit [1, 0]",       lambda: run(read([1, 0]), ["c1", "c0"])),
    ("read, emit [5]",          lambda: run(read([5]), ["x"])),
    ("read, emit [-1]",         lambda: run(read([-1]), ["x"])),
    ("project, emit [5]",       lambda: run({"project": dict(
                                    {"input": read(), "expressions": [ref(0)]},
                                    **emit([5]))}, ["x"])),
    ("aggregate, emit [1, 0]",  lambda: run(AGG, ["c1", "c0"])),
]

label, case = VARIANTS[int(sys.argv[1])]
print("%-22s" % label, end=" ", flush=True)
try:
    print(case().read_all().schema.types)
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__ + ":", str(e).replace("\n", " ")[:70])
```

</details>

issues.title: [Python] Categorical boolean column saved as regular boolean in parquet
issues.body:
When saving a pandas dataframe to parquet, if there is a categorical column where the categories are boolean, the column is saved as regular boolean.

This causes an issue because, when reading back the parquet file, I expect the column to still be categorical.

 
Reproducible example:
```python

import pandas as pd
import pyarrow

# Create dataframe with boolean column that is then converted to categorical
df = pd.DataFrame({'a': [True, True, False, True, False]})
df['a'] = df['a'].astype('category')

# Convert to arrow Table and save to disk
table = pyarrow.Table.from_pandas(df)
pyarrow.parquet.write_table(table, 'test.parquet')

# Reload data and convert back to pandas
table_rel = pyarrow.parquet.read_table('test.parquet')
df_rel = table_rel.to_pandas()
```

The arrow `table` variable correctly converts the column to an arrow `DICTIONARY` type:
```

>>> df['a']
0     True
1     True
2    False
3     True
4    False
Name: a, dtype: category
Categories (2, object): [False, True]
>>>
>>> table
pyarrow.Table
a: dictionary<values=bool, indices=int8, ordered=0>
```

However, the reloaded column is now a regular boolean:
```

>>> table_rel
pyarrow.Table
a: bool
>>>
>>> df_rel['a']
0     True
1     True
2    False
3     True
4    False
Name: a, dtype: bool
```

I would have expected the column to be read back as categorical.


**Reporter**: [Joao Moreira](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/ARROW-13342)
#### Related issues:
- [[C++][Parquet] Support direct dictionary decoding of types other than BYTE_ARRAY](https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/22534) (is blocked by)
- [[Python] Consistent handling of categoricals](https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/27067) (is related to)

<sub>**Note**: *This issue was originally created as [ARROW-13342](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/ARROW-13342). Please see the [migration documentation](https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/14542) for further details.*</sub>

comments.body:
[Alessandro Molina](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/ARROW-13342?focusedCommentId=17382081) / @amol-:
FYI, this seems to happen for numeric types. The same is true for `int` and `double`

```Java

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet

# Convert to arrow Table and save to disk
table = pa.Table.from_arrays([
    pa.DictionaryArray.from_arrays(indices=pa.array([0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0], type=pa.int8()), 
                                   dictionary=[10000000000000000, 20000000000000000])
], names=["data"])
print(table)
pa.parquet.write_table(table, 'test.parquet')

# Reload data and convert back to pandas
table_rel = pa.parquet.read_table('test.parquet')
print(table_rel)
```

The exception seem to be `unicode` which preserves the dictionary form.  

In general, from my understanding, it seems arrow currently writes in dictionary form only the binary types ( https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/14b75ee71d770ba86999e0e7a0e0b94629b91968/cpp/src/parquet/column_writer.cc#L1008 )

This in general seems a fairly reasonable behaviour to me, because in general binary data/text is where you get most saving due to the delta in size between the data and the indices.

On the other side, I don't think that "preserving same exact type" that was provided to a writer is an expectation that can be always satisfied or that it makes sense to enforce. In some cases enforcing dictionary encoding because the input was dictionary encoded might lead to bigger parquet files, or for some types for example that might not even be possible, think of CSV or JSON, not all types can be represented in those formats and thus the data you read back might have a different type

[Weston Pace](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/ARROW-13342?focusedCommentId=17382271) / @westonpace:
Judging by ARROW-3246 I believe the original intent was to support more types than just the binary types.  Also, Arrow is supposed to be storing custom metadata (arrow:SCHEMA) in the parquet file with details on the original Arrow schema.  This way, if we need to store the data more efficiently then we can do so while still restoring the original types upon deserialization.  I checked and store_schema is set to true and it does properly decode and restore the original schema which does report the column "a" as dictionary<values=bool, indices=int8, ordered=0>.  I'm not sure if some linkage is broken or if it only tries to restore the metadata on binary types.

 

However, I think the resolution for this issue is (although maybe not easy), the existing mechanism should be extended to handle more types.

comments.body:
[Joris Van den Bossche](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/ARROW-13342?focusedCommentId=17382497) / @jorisvandenbossche:
Directly reading dictionary encoded data in Parquet as dictionary typed arrays in Arrow is currently indeed only supported for BYTE_ARRAY storage (i.e. string, binary). The issue tracking the follow-up to expand this support to other data types is ARROW-6140.

The documentation of `pq.read_table` also somewhat mentions this:

```Java

read_dictionary : list, default None
    List of names or column paths (for nested types) to read directly
    as DictionaryArray. Only supported for BYTE_ARRAY storage. 
    ...
```

This parameter allows to explicitly specify which columns to read as dictionary arrays. But it doesn't mention the default behaviour, which is to infer those columns from the stored arrow:SCHEMA.

issues.title: [C++] arrow::csv silently drops one byte when a CRLF inside a quoted field straddles a parser block boundary
issues.body:
### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.

`arrow::csv` silently drops one byte when a CRLF inside a quoted field straddles a parser
block boundary. The `\r` is kept and the `\n` disappears. No error, no warning — the value
simply comes back one byte shorter than it was written.

This reproduces on **Arrow C++ `main`**, in C++, with no Python in the picture, and at the
**shipped default block size** with no options tuned.

**Build under test**

```
Arrow C++ main @ 0bd8def  ("GH-51343: [C++][CI][Packaging] Disable Precompile Headers
                            on simdjson...", 2026-09-17)
libarrow.so.2600.0.0, 26.0.0-SNAPSHOT, Release build
cmake 4.4.3 / g++ 11.4.0 / Ubuntu 22.04 x86_64
```

Also reproduces on released **pyarrow 25.0.1** (newest on PyPI), on all three entry points —
`csv.read_csv`, the streaming `csv.open_csv`, and the dataset API — which is what places it
in the shared reader rather than in a wrapper.

**Minimal case.** A CSV whose row 0 holds a quoted value containing one embedded CRLF.
`newlines_in_values = true` is required for such a file; without it the reader rejects the
file outright (`Expected 3 columns, got 2`) rather than corrupting it.

```
id,s,p
0,"zzzz…zzzA<CR><LF>B",x
1,plain,x
2,plain,x
```

Walking that CRLF one byte at a time across a 1024-byte block boundary, 1028 offsets tried
on `main`:

```
block_size = 1024, walking one embedded CRLF across the boundary

  pad=1012: CR at byte 1023, LF at byte 1024, boundary at 1024
    wrote 1016B ...A\r\n   read 1015B ...zA\r

1 corrupting offset(s), 0 error(s), out of 1028 tried.
```

Exactly one offset out of 1028: the one where **the CR is the last byte of a block and the
LF is the first byte of the next**.

**It is not an artefact of a small block size.** With no `ReadOptions` at all, so the shipped
1 MiB block applies, on `main`:

```
 file bytes  CR at byte  verdict
    1048602     1048575  CORRUPT: LF silently dropped
    1048603     1048576  ok
    1048604     1048577  ok
    1048605     1048578  ok
    1048606     1048579  ok
```

**It is specific to the CR–LF pair.** Same sweep on `main`, varying the byte sequence placed
inside the quoted field (1032 offsets each):

| sequence inside the quoted field | corrupting offsets |
|---|---:|
| `A\r\nB` (embedded CRLF) | **1** |
| `A\r\r\nB` (CR CR LF) | **1** |
| `A\nB` (lone LF) | 0 |
| `A\rB` (lone CR) | 0 |
| `A\n\rB` (LF then CR) | 0 |
| `A€B` (3-byte UTF-8) | 0 |

A lone `\n` or a lone `\r` at exactly the same boundary survives; only the two sequences that
contain a `\r` immediately followed by `\n` lose a byte, and the CR-CR-LF case is the same
defect one byte over. So this is not general boundary mishandling — the doubled-quote escape
and multi-byte UTF-8 paths are sound across the boundary.

### Reproduction

**C++ (this is the one that runs against `main`).** Build Arrow with `-DARROW_CSV=ON`, then:

```cpp
#include <arrow/csv/api.h>
#include <arrow/io/api.h>
#include <arrow/table.h>
#include <arrow/array.h>
#include <fstream>
#include <cstdio>

int main() {
  const std::string PREFIX = "id,s,p\n0,\"", VAL = "A\r\nB", PATH = "/tmp/f.csv";
  const int block = 1024;
  for (int pad = block - 1020; pad < block + 8; pad++) {
    { std::ofstream f(PATH, std::ios::binary);
      f << PREFIX << std::string(pad, 'z') << VAL << "\",x\n1,plain,x\n2,plain,x\n"; }
    auto file = arrow::io::ReadableFile::Open(PATH).ValueOrDie();
    auto ro = arrow::csv::ReadOptions::Defaults();  ro.block_size = block;
    auto po = arrow::csv::ParseOptions::Defaults(); po.newlines_in_values = true;
    auto co = arrow::csv::ConvertOptions::Defaults();
    co.column_types = {{"id", arrow::int32()}, {"s", arrow::utf8()}, {"p", arrow::utf8()}};
    auto table = arrow::csv::TableReader::Make(arrow::io::default_io_context(), file,
                                               ro, po, co).ValueOrDie()->Read().ValueOrDie();
    auto col = table->GetColumnByName("s");
    std::string got;
    for (int i = 0; i < col->num_chunks(); i++) {
      auto a = std::static_pointer_cast<arrow::StringArray>(col->chunk(i));
      if (a->length() > 0) { got = a->GetString(0); break; }
    }
    std::string want = std::string(pad, 'z') + VAL;
    if (got != want)
      printf("pad=%d: wrote %zuB, read %zuB -> LF dropped\n", pad, want.size(), got.size());
  }
}
```

Prints exactly one line, at `pad=1012`. Drop `ro.block_size = block` and use
`pad = (1<<20) - PREFIX.size() - 2` to see the same at the shipped default.

**Python (released pyarrow 25.0.1), for convenience:**

```python
import pyarrow as pa, pyarrow.csv as pc

PREFIX, VAL = b'id,s,p\n0,"', "A\r\nB"

def check(pad, block):
    with open("/tmp/f.csv", "wb") as fh:
        fh.write(PREFIX + b"z" * pad + VAL.encode() + b'",x\n1,plain,x\n2,plain,x\n')
    t = pc.read_csv("/tmp/f.csv",
                    read_options=pc.ReadOptions(block_size=block) if block else pc.ReadOptions(),
                    parse_options=pc.ParseOptions(newlines_in_values=True),
                    convert_options=pc.ConvertOptions(
                        column_types={"id": pa.int32(), "s": pa.string(), "p": pa.string()}))
    return t.column("s").to_pylist()[0] == "z" * pad + VAL

print(check(1012, 1024))            # False  <- LF dropped
print(check((1 << 20) - len(PREFIX) - 2, None))   # False, at the shipped 1 MiB block
```

`polars` and `duckdb` read the identical bytes back correctly, so the file is well formed and
this is the reader, not the writer.

### Where it comes from (a lead, not a confirmed diagnosis)

I have not bisected this to a single line, but the shape of the failure matches a specific
pattern that appears in both the chunker and the parser: a `\r` handler that looks ahead one
byte for the `\n` and gives up if the byte is not in the current buffer.

`cpp/src/arrow/csv/chunker.cc`, in the lexer's unquoted-field path:

```cpp
if (ARROW_PREDICT_FALSE(c == '\r')) {
  if (ARROW_PREDICT_TRUE(data != data_end) && *data == '\n') {
    data++;
  }
  goto LineEnd;      // CR at the end of the buffer => treated as a complete terminator
}
```

`cpp/src/arrow/csv/parser.cc` has the same look-ahead guard (`data < data_end && *data ==
'\n'`), and additionally treats a `\n` that is the *first* byte it sees as an empty line:

```cpp
// Special case empty lines: do we start with a newline separator?
c = *data;
if (ARROW_PREDICT_FALSE(IsControlChar(c))) {
  ...
  if (c == '\n') {
    data++;
    goto EmptyLine;
  }
}
```

A CR that ends a buffer is therefore accepted as a whole line terminator, and the orphaned LF
that opens the next buffer is then consumed as a separator rather than as data. That is
consistent with every observation above: it needs the pair, it needs the split to fall
between the two bytes, and a lone CR or lone LF at the same offset is unaffected.

`FindFirstInternal` in `chunker.cc` runs the lexer over `partial` and then over `block`
(`cpp/src/arrow/csv/chunker.cc`, `LexingBoundaryFinder`), which is the seam where the
carried-over state would need to remember "the previous buffer ended on a CR" for the pair to
be reassembled.

### Describe the bug, including details regarding any error messages, version, and platform.

## Summary

`pyarrow.Table.join()` crashes my Python session when 1 or more `large_string` columns are used as keys, and the data in those columns nears 2gb.  
Specifically, we can use the following inequality to define the bound of where this bug occurs

> occurs when: `[num_rows]*[num_keys]*([key_length]+9) > [2 gigabytes]`
> In words: if the amount of key data plus the additional 9 bytes per key exceeds 2gb, a fatal crash occurs.  

I focused my investigation on 'left anti' joins, where the right table is near boundary, in which case the left table's size seems irrelevant.  Just before submission, I confirmed that this occurs with all join types when tested with a large right table.

### Expected Behaviour

The table join function should support the use of `large_string` columns of any size as keys.  

### Actual Behaviour

The join function causes a fatal crash when `large_string` key columns exceed a certain size which is below, but near, 2gb.  

## Tested With

PyArrow versions tested: 
- `24.0.1`
- `25.0.0`
- `26.0.0`

Platform:
- Windows
- Linux

## Investigation

I suspect there is an `int32_t` where there may need to be something larger.  The stack trace leads to the C++ method `arrow.compute.internal.RowEncoder.EncodeAndAppend()` (found in [row_encoder_internal.cc](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/1776578067602ed059db9bd8c3e4fc126c4597f3/cpp/src/arrow/compute/row/row_encoder_internal.cc#L358)).  This method makes use of a private member, `offsets_`, which is defined in [row_encoder_internal.h](https://github.com/apache/arrow/blob/1776578067602ed059db9bd8c3e4fc126c4597f3/cpp/src/arrow/compute/row/row_encoder_internal.h#L397) and contains the following note

```cpp
// offsets_ vector stores the starting position (offset) of each encoded row
  // within the bytes_ vector. This allows for quick access to individual rows.
  //
  // The size would be num_rows + 1 if not empty, the last element is the total
  // length of the bytes_ vector.
  std::vector<int32_t> offsets_;
```

This has me wondering, if the bytes vector exceeds a certain size, will the offset not be able to address it?
